newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jerusalem mayor says he's innocent in funds case.
newsitem.headline: Jerusalem mayor says he's innocent in funds case.

text.p: Jerusalem's Jewish Mayor Ehud Olmert said on Friday he was innocent of charges filed against him in connection with an alleged 1988 campaign funding fraud.
"I unequivocally claim complete innocence. I am convinced that will be proved," said Olmert, a leading figure in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party.
Court spokesman Moshe Gorali said that prosecutors filed charges against Olmert in Tel Aviv District Court on Thursday.

A charge sheet obtained by Reuters said Olmert "intentionally misled the State Comptroller" by "hiding the fact that the Likud received, against the provisions of the Campaign Funding Law, contributions from Israeli corporations".
It alleged that Olmert, then party treasurer, and other Likud financial officers created a fictitious public relations firm to receive and disguise donations from corporations.
Election laws bar direct or indirect corporate contributions to political parties.
The charges do not accuse Olmert of reaping personal financial gain from the contributions.
A close political ally of Netanyahu, Olmert has long been under investigation over the allegations.

Political commentators have said that Olmert, a senior minister and high-profile government spokesman during the former Likud administration of Yitzhak Shamir, was denied a cabinet post by Netanyahu over the funding affair.
The prosecution submitted a list of more than 100 witnesses it expected to call during the trial, among them two former Likud cabinet ministers.
Olmert, 51, won an upset victory in November 1993 over octogenarian Teddy Kollek, who had been mayor of the volatile holy city for more than 27 years.

Israel captured and annexed Arab East Jerusalem in 1967. Palestinians living in East Jerusalem have long refused to vote in municipal elections. The international community does not recognise the annexation.
Throughout the years-long investigation, Olmert has consistently maintained he is innocent.
In the past, trials of public figures on corruption or fraud charges have commonly lasted for several years.
State-run Israel Television's Channel One quoted Olmert as rejecting calls by opposition lawmakers for the mayor to remove himself from office for the duration of the trial.
"I have no intention of suspending myself, there is no legal reason, public justification, no precedent for doing so," he said.
Legal authority Moshe Negbi said the law was unclear on the suspension issue for mayors charged with crimes and the Supreme Court might be asked to rule on the question.
